rv.q: Is Al Pacino, who is 75, really reading his lines off concealed teleprompters? Over and above the gossip, it’s a matter of humiliating record that “The Anarchist,” Mr. Mamet’s last play, crashed and burned three years ago, closing on Broadway after 17 performances, while the one that preceded it in 2009, “Race,” was good enough but not up to form.
And while the Oscar- and Tony-winner is impossible to stop watching -- the play itself is a meandering one-note character study of a doomed man.
It is hard to imagine a more disorienting show.
The playwright has given Pacino almost no story to build around his character and given him lines that pick over the same obvious plot points.
But even with Al Pacino putting him through his emotional paces, this tarnished titan is going through hell in a vacuum, with no one to play off but unheard voices on the other end of the telephone.
China Doll offers the sad spectacle of two world-class artists turning in their lamest work.
In the meantime, Al Pacino, for whom the role was written, huffs and puffs his way through a performance that remains oddly tentative despite all the showboating mannerisms.
Al Pacino’s querulous lion routine pulls in the crowd but he’s doomed to repeat the same old shtick in Mamet’s lacklustre Broadway transfer
China Doll, his shaky new Broadway vehicle, by David Mamet, offers flashes of that brilliance between long mucky passages in which he appears to be hunting for the narrative, if not the next line.

Whatever Mamet's points, he and Pacino consistently engage us -- which is more than you can say for a lot of the folks the playwright is targeting here.

David Mamet has written a devastating portrait of a David Koch/Sheldon Adelson-style tycoon whose deep pockets fund at least one prominent governor...There's only one other character in the play, Ross' assistant (Christopher Denham), who is merely a prop for most of the play's two hours -- until he becomes something much more...
If China Doll has its weaknesses--and it has--it also has Al Pacino.
Plays depending on phone conversations with unseen participants are almost always a bad idea, and China Doll is no exception.
“China Doll” is muddled, but it's still a treat to see Pacino, even if we're not always sure what he's doing.
Pacino, looking somewhat frail and moving slowly, delivers his lines in a near-whisper that forces audience members to lean forward and strain to hear him.
So why bother to write a play for him?
China Doll is less a play than a very expensive therapy session that we've been forced to attend.
Despite the play’s problems, Pacino’s theatrics throw it off further dramatically.

"'China Doll' is not even better than oral surgery. At least for that sort of medical procedure you get painkillers. And it’s not a complete waste of time and money...Pacino is Mickey Ross, who’s on his cellphone for three-quarters of the show. Not the stuff of great drama...

If CHINA DOLL doesn't set off the sparks of a SPEED-THE-PLOW or an OLEANNA, it does provide enough of the old Mamet tension and cynicism that makes decent people feel disgust for the world we live in.
It's an intriguing lion-in-winter performance, one that captures both the vanity and tragedy of a giant trying to hang onto his old glory.

That’s more than can be said for the rest of the play, which, given the price of tickets, resembles for most theatergoers the experience of paying for an internship as Donald Trump’s lackey, forced to witness the conversations of a madman without the luxury of exasperated interruption.
First of all, David Mamet’s script is nearly lifeless.
China Doll is an exasperating spectacle of poor writing and dispirited stellar performing that comes close to being an outright debacle.
